t: Minimum Sideway Jumps — Rolling DP Across Three Lanes
o:
**Understanding the problem**

A frog starts on lane 2 at point 0 and must reach point n on any lane. Between adjacent points it advances on its current lane if that lane is clear at the next point; within a point it may side-jump to any other obstacle-free lane — adjacent or not — for a cost of 1. We minimize total side jumps. obstacles[i] names the single blocked lane at point i (0 = clear), and both endpoints are guaranteed clear. Example 1 ([0,1,2,3,0]) costs 2: ride lane 2 to point 1, hop to lane 3, ride to point 3, then hop off lane 3 before entering the obstacle there. Example 2 ([0,1,1,3,3,0]) costs 0 because lane 2 is never blocked. Length up to 10^5 demands a linear sweep; with only three lanes, one minimum-cost counter per lane suffices.
k: State is (point, lane) but there are just 3 lanes, so a 3-value rolling minimum swept left to right captures everything.
Arriving at a point is free; a side jump costs 1 and may cross to ANY clear lane at that point, so each point relaxes every lane toward the current best.
Blocked lanes are barred from both arrival and jump targets, and the answer is the cheapest lane at the final point.

a.n: Approach 1: Dijkstra on the State Graph
a.i: Model every (point, lane) cell as a node. Add zero-cost edges forward along a clear lane and unit-cost edges between clear lanes of the same point. Dijkstra from (point 0, lane 2) then yields minimum jump counts everywhere, and the first node popped at point n settles the answer. General and hard to get wrong, at the cost of a priority queue and a full distance table.
s: Set dist[0][lane 2] = 0 and push it; all other distances are infinite.
Pop the cheapest state; if its point is n, return its cost.
Relax the forward edge to (point + 1, lane) when that lane is unblocked at point + 1, costing 0.
Relax same-point edges to each other unblocked lane, costing 1.
a.t: O(n log n) — about 3n nodes with a handful of heap pushes each, logarithmic per operation
a.sp: O(n) for the distance table and queue

a.i: Let dp[l] be the fewest jumps to be standing at the current point on lane l, seeded as [1, 0, 1] at point 0 (starting on lane 2, reaching lanes 1 or 3 costs one jump each). Moving to the next point: a blocked lane becomes unreachable (infinite); then, since every lane may jump to any other at the same point for one jump, set each unblocked lane to min(dp[l], best + 1), where best is the smallest current value. One linear pass completes the computation.
s: For each point i: if obstacles[i] = b, set dp[b - 1] = infinity.
Compute best = min(dp); for each lane l not blocked at i, set dp[l] = min(dp[l], best + 1).
Return min(dp) after processing the final point.
a.t: O(n) — constant work (three lanes) per point

w:
**Wrap-up**

Present the rolling DP in interviews; fall back to Dijkstra only if you reason in graphs and want extra safety. Pitfalls: allowing a jump to land on the newly blocked lane (the l + 1 != obstacle guard is essential), applying best + 1 to a blocked lane, and reporting a specific lane instead of the minimum over lanes. Ordering inside a point matters: first invalidate arrivals onto the obstacle, then relax jumps using the fresh best. Follow-up: with L lanes and several obstacles per point, the same recurrence works using an ordered multiset of lane costs to fetch the two best values in O(log L).
